items.text: A monthly mortgage payment bundles several charges together, and they don't all go to the same place. Part of it is the loan itself, which goes to the lender. The rest is money the borrower owes to other people entirely — it only passes through the lender on its way out the door.

The loan itself comes down to a simple deal. The borrower took a large sum to buy the home, and now pays it back over the years, plus a charge for the use of the money. Those two pieces are the principal and the interest. Principal is the amount actually borrowed — the balance still owed. Interest is what it costs to borrow it: the lender's charge for letting you use the money, quoted as an annual percentage. Only part of each payment reduces the principal. The rest is interest, and none of the interest ever comes back to you. Here's the fact that shapes everything else: interest is charged on the balance still outstanding. Not on what you originally borrowed. On what's left.

A standard mortgage is amortizing. You make level payments, and by the end the balance reaches zero. But the split inside those level payments shifts the whole way through. Because interest is charged on the balance, and the balance starts high, the early payments are mostly interest, with only a sliver going to principal. As the balance shrinks the mix tips the other way, until the late payments are mostly principal. Now — this loan is not a law of nature. It's an invention, and a fairly recent one. Before nineteen thirty-three, the standard American home loan ran five to ten years, the borrower paid interest only, and the entire principal came due at the end in one enormous balloon payment. You refinanced, or you lost the house. By the spring of nineteen thirty-three the country was running close to a thousand foreclosures a day. The federal government stepped in, refinanced about a million mortgages, and standardized the fully amortizing loan you just learned. The term is how long the loan is scheduled to run — a thirty-year and a fifteen-year loan of the same amount are the same debt stretched over different lengths. A shorter term means a higher monthly payment, but far less total interest.

Principal and interest are the loan. But most borrowers' monthly checks cover more than that. The shorthand is PITI — principal, interest, taxes, and insurance. The taxes are the property taxes owed to the local government. The insurance is the homeowners policy. Rather than leave a borrower to save up for one big annual tax or insurance bill, the servicer collects a twelfth of those costs with each payment and holds the money in an escrow account, then pays the tax authority and the insurer directly when the bills come due. So two of PITI's four letters never belong to the lender at all. Taxes and insurance only pass through.
